1 · Cell temperature

The plotted curve is an illustrative exponential I–V curve scaled so its maximum power equals the model's P_dc. The simulation itself uses the P_dc equation.

  1. Photons with enough energy knock electrons across the p–n junction in each cell, giving a photocurrent proportional to irradiance.
  2. The junction also behaves as a diode, so the terminal current falls off exponentially as voltage rises toward V_oc: the I–V knee.
  3. Heat lowers the voltage (about −0.27 %/K per cell) and so the power (−0.40 %/K): a hot day yields less than a cold one at the same irradiance.
  4. Twelve modules in series raise the voltage to about 490 V at the maximum power point; two strings in parallel double the current. Bypass diodes in each junction box let current skip shaded cell groups.
  5. The inverter's MPPT holds the operating point near the knee of the curve.

Silicon cells turn light into DC electricity. The array is 24 modules in two strings; its output follows irradiance and falls as the cells heat up.

Modules24 × 500 Wp monocrystalline, 60 cells, 2.28 × 1.13 m, 28 kg
Strings2 × 12 in series; V_mp ≈ 490 V, V_oc ≈ 590 V, I_mp ≈ 25 A total

Junction box3 bypass diodes, IP68, 4 mm² cables with MC4 connectors
StructureFour galvanised posts, flat canopy, 2.8 m clearance, M16 × 4 per post

η = P_ac / P_dc, P_ac ≤ P_r

6 · MPPT (perturb and observe)
V_(k+1) = V_k + ΔV · sign(ΔP · ΔV)

Only the first two equations drive the simulation; the others describe the mechanism.

  1. A DC–DC boost stage lifts the array voltage to a regulated 700 V DC link held by electrolytic capacitors.
  2. Six IGBTs form a three-phase bridge. A carrier (8 kHz triangle) is compared with a 50 Hz sine reference; the comparator output switches each leg.
  3. The LCL filter smooths the switched voltage into a sinusoidal current. A phase-locked loop keeps the current in phase with the grid.
  4. MPPT perturbs the operating voltage and keeps the direction that raised power (perturb-and-observe).
  5. Losses are conduction, switching and standby; they rise with power, so efficiency peaks at mid-load and clips at the AC rating.

A grid-tied inverter converts the array's DC into 400 V three-phase AC, tracks the maximum power point, and disconnects if the grid fails.

The indicator diagram uses the model's clearance, effective exponent and pressure ratio. Its enclosed area gives an independent power estimate (ideal gas), compared with the table-based isentropic power: a cross-check, not an input.

  1. Down-stroke: the piston falls, cylinder pressure drops below suction pressure and the suction reed lifts: vapour flows in.
  2. Up-stroke: both reeds close and the trapped vapour is compressed along a polytropic curve.
  3. When cylinder pressure exceeds discharge pressure the discharge reed lifts and the vapour leaves.
  4. At top dead centre a little gas remains in the clearance volume; it expands on the next down-stroke before suction can start. That lost part of the stroke is why volumetric efficiency falls as pressure ratio rises.
  5. The VFD changes motor speed; mass flow is proportional to speed.

An open-drive reciprocating compressor draws low-pressure vapour in, squeezes it to the condenser pressure and pushes it out. The motor turns a crank that moves the piston.

States shown: idle, room cooling, charging the ice bank.

  1. A diode rectifier converts 400 V AC to about 566 V DC; the choke and capacitors smooth it.
  2. An IGBT inverter chops the DC bus into pulses whose width follows a sine; the motor sees an AC voltage with frequency f and proportional amplitude (V/f control).
  3. The controller reads room, evaporator and condenser temperatures and the PV output, then picks a mode and speed.
  4. Solar-priority: choose the highest speed whose total draw fits the PV output; otherwise run only when the room needs it.
  5. Protection: any trip opens the contactor; minimum on and off times protect the compressor.

The drive turns fixed-frequency mains into variable-frequency power for the motor, and the controller decides when and how fast to run.

Tube colours show how many of the 24 drawn tube ends belong to each zone (red desuperheating, green condensing, blue subcooling).

  1. Superheated vapour enters at the top row of tubes and first cools to saturation (desuperheating, a small share of the heat).
  2. At saturation it condenses at nearly constant temperature, giving up latent heat (the largest share).
  3. The last tubes subcool the liquid by about 3 K so the expansion valve receives no vapour.
  4. An EC fan pulls air across the finned coil; fan speed follows heat rejection, and head-pressure control prevents condensing below 20 °C in cold weather.
  5. Condensing temperature settles where heat rejected equals UA × (T_c − T_amb).

Hot vapour from the compressor gives up its heat to outdoor air and becomes liquid. The air-cooled coil has three zones: desuperheating, condensing and subcooling.

The liquid level in the receiver is illustrative: refrigerant inventory is not modelled.

  1. Liquid from the condenser enters the receiver, falls to the bottom and leaves through a dip tube, so only liquid goes to the valve.
  2. A relief valve on the shell opens above 21 bar(g) and a sight glass shows liquid and moisture.
  3. In the valve, liquid squeezes through a small orifice at the needle seat; the pressure falls to evaporator pressure and part of it flashes to vapour (state 4).
  4. A sensing bulb clamped to the suction line holds a charge whose pressure follows the suction temperature. It acts on the diaphragm: higher superheat opens the needle, lower superheat closes it.
  5. A spring sets the superheat at 5 K; the needle's lift follows the required mass flow.

The receiver stores liquid refrigerant. The thermostatic expansion valve meters it into the evaporator and creates the high-to-low pressure drop.

Tube colours: blue evaporating, red superheating.

  1. The valve delivers a cold two-phase mixture to a distributor that feeds the coil circuits evenly.
  2. Room air flows through the finned coil; the refrigerant boils at nearly constant temperature T_e, well below the air temperature.
  3. Near the outlet the last tubes superheat the vapour by about 5 K, so no liquid reaches the compressor.
  4. The fans add a little heat to the room; the drain pan collects condensate and a heater rod removes frost (defrost is not modelled).
  5. Evaporating temperature settles where the coil's heat transfer matches the compressor's capacity.

Liquid refrigerant boils inside the coil and absorbs heat from the room air that fans pull through it.

Ice volume is proportional to state of charge, hence the square-root radius law. The store is active only in the solar-plus-store mode.

  1. Refrigerant boils inside six vertical coil tubes, cooling the surrounding brine below its −4 °C melt point.
  2. Ice grows outward from each tube as a growing annulus; the section view shows the radius rising with state of charge.
  3. Charging forces a lower evaporating temperature than room cooling, so COP is lower: that cost is traded for using solar energy that would otherwise be exported.
  4. When the room warms above 2 °C a pump circulates brine to the room and a proportional valve sets the discharge, up to 8 kW.
  5. The tank's insulation and the standing loss slowly melt the ice even if unused.

When there is spare solar power the compressor freezes brine around coils in a tank. At night the ice melts and cools the room, so the compressor can stay off.

Export price is $0.04/kWh.

  1. Power enters through the service drop to a main breaker, RCD and surge protection, then a busbar.
  2. Current transformers on each phase feed the meter, which integrates power into separate import and export registers.
  3. The inverter feeds the same busbar: solar goes to loads first, any surplus flows out through the meter, any shortfall comes in.
  4. The tariff changes through the day: cheap at night, expensive from 17:00 to 21:00.
  5. If the grid is opened (detached), the plant is islanded and the compressor runs only on PV.

The utility supply and a bidirectional meter balance whatever solar cannot cover, and record what is exported.

The analytic warm-up is reproduced by the simulation to 0.01 K (test_room_free_decay_matches_analytic).

  1. Heat leaks through the walls in proportion to the temperature difference to outside (UA_env).
  2. Deliveries and handling add a process load during working hours, with random pulses.
  3. The unit cooler fans add heat while running; the coil and the ice bank remove it.
  4. The room's air, product and racking store heat: its large thermal mass lets temperature drift slowly, so the plant can wait for solar power.
  5. The solar-priority policies exploit this by pre-cooling to 0.5 °C and coasting up toward 3.5 °C.

The insulated room is the load and the thermal flywheel: it gains heat from outside and from product handling, and loses it to the coil and the ice bank.

Simulated, simplified model (see the paper). Live page and Python agree to <1e-3 kWh on the reference day (web/parity.mjs).

Mean and spread over 16 identical days: grid import, cost and compressor starts.

Sensitivity to store size, solar availability, demand variability and ambient temperature.

Reference day: irradiance and ambient, room temperature, grid import and ice-bank charge for the three policies.

Grid saving against the fixed policy for store size and solar availability.

What to read from it

  • The store raises electricity use but cuts grid use and cost, because the extra energy is solar.
  • Returns from store size diminish after about 20 kWh.
  • Part of the solar-priority saving comes from the wider room band (0.5 to 3.5 °C) and partial-speed running; the baseline is a plain thermostat.
  • Demand variability had a small effect; hotter ambient reduces the benefit.

Verification

  • 15 Python tests: heat rejection = cooling + shaft work, room and store energy balances close to 1e-6, electrical accounting, analytic room warm-up, constraints, detached-module behaviour.
  • Browser model equals Python reference (≤ 2e-4); JS-built map equals the Python map to 5e-5.
